v.q: What is a cross-cutting concern that AOP is designed to handle?
o: Logging, security checks or transactions applied across many classes
The main business rule of a single service
The schema of a single database table
The layout of one web page
v.w: AOP lets you write such behaviour once and apply it to many methods without touching their code.

v.q: Which concern is NOT a good candidate for AOP?
v.w: AOP suits repeated concerns across many classes. Core business logic belongs in the service itself.

v.q: How does Spring AOP apply advice to a bean?
o: It wraps the bean in a runtime proxy that runs advice around calls
It rewrites the bytecode of the class on disk
It copies the method body into every caller
It uses reflection to edit private fields
v.w: Spring uses JDK dynamic proxies for interfaces and CGLIB subclass proxies otherwise. AspectJ weaving is a separate, heavier option.

v.q: Which statement about Spring AOP is NOT true?
o: It rewrites class files on disk
v.w: Spring AOP creates proxies at run time. Bytecode weaving, as in AspectJ, is a different approach.

v.q: `OrderService.place()` calls `this.audit()`, which carries an `@Audited` aspect. Why is the aspect skipped?
o: The call on `this` bypasses the proxy, so the advice never runs
Aspects can only ever be applied to static methods
`@Audited` is ignored whenever it sits on a public method
Spring caches only the very first call of each method
v.w: Self-invocation is the classic proxy pitfall. Move the method to another bean or inject the proxy.

v.q: Which call reaches the aspect on a Spring bean?
v.w: Only calls that go through the proxy are advised. Self-invocation skips it.

v.q: Which advice type runs whether the method returns normally or throws an exception?
v.w: `@Around` is the most powerful: it controls whether and how the target runs, and can change the result.

v.q: Which advice type runs only when the method throws?
v.w: @AfterThrowing runs on an exception. @After runs in both cases.

v.q: In an `@Around` advice, what happens if you never call `proceed()`?
o: The target method does not run
Spring calls it after the advice finishes
An exception is thrown at startup
v.w: That is how caching and security aspects short-circuit a call. Remember to return the value from `proceed()`.

v.q: An @Around advice calls proceed() twice. What happens?
v.w: Each proceed() invokes the next advice or the target again, which is how retry aspects work.

o: An expression that selects which join points the advice applies to
The block of code that always runs before a method starts
A breakpoint that is set in the debugger by a developer
A configuration file that tells Spring how to build proxies
v.w: Example: `execution(* com.bank.service..*.*(..))` matches every method in the service package.
A pointcut expression says which method executions the advice applies to.

v.q: Which Spring features are implemented with AOP proxies?
v.w: They all intercept method calls through a proxy, so they share the same limits: public methods, called through the bean reference.

v.q: Which feature does NOT use an AOP proxy?
v.w: Injection is done by the container when it builds the bean. The others wrap method calls.

v.q: A `private` method is annotated `@Transactional`. What happens with Spring's proxy-based AOP?
o: The annotation has no effect, since proxies skip private calls
The transaction starts normally, just as the developer expected
The application fails to start with a configuration error
The method silently becomes public so the proxy can reach it
v.w: Proxy-based AOP cannot intercept private methods or self-invocation. Use public methods on a separate bean.

v.q: Which method does Spring proxy-based AOP NOT advise?
o: A public method called from another bean
A public method on an interface
A protected method on a CGLIB proxy
v.w: Private methods cannot be overridden or called through the proxy.
